## APRV-423 — a harness cap on the request, and a TTL that lapses before it

A harness holds a tool call for a bounded time (Hermes will not let a `pre_tool_call` entry be configured past 300s at all) and the policy TTL is usually hours, so a request stayed grantable long after the harness had stopped holding the call: a tap in between produced an `approval.granted` for a call nobody had.

A hook-originated `approval.requested` now carries `harness_cap_ms`, the **duration** its harness can hold the call, folded by `core/harness-wait.ts` from the ceiling this project documents for that harness and the operator's own `--harness-cap`. `HARNESS_PROCESS_CAP_MS` names a number for hermes alone (300000, its documented per-entry maximum) and `null` everywhere else, because the other harnesses document a default rather than a ceiling and a guess in the one place a deadline is computed from is worse than no number.

The narrowing is applied in the **lazy judge**, and that placement is the design: `core/state.ts`'s `requestState` reads the field off the request's own record and judges the lapse against `min(policy TTL, cap - 60s)`, so the grant path, `expire`, the daemon sweep, the queue renderer and the channel all read one answer and SPEC §10.2's "the sweep changes no verdict" still holds. The margin is two `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS`, because a sweep appends somewhere in `[lapse, lapse + interval]` and one interval would let the append land on the cap rather than before it.

Invariants: the cap reaches the TTL only through a `min` against the policy TTL, so it narrows and never widens (§11.1 invariant 4); it is a duration and never an instant, so the deadline comes from the record's runtime-assigned `ts` (invariant 2); no frozen union gains a member (invariant 6) — a late tap takes the existing `expired` and `hook-expired`, whose message now names the cap. No schema change: the v0.1 payload is open and the shape is enforced at the write boundary.

On hermes the effective TTL is 240s, the same instant as its documented `--timeout 4m`, so APRV-287's retry grace has no room on that harness and a retry asks fresh. That is the arithmetic of a 300-second ceiling rather than a choice made here, and `docs/hermes-hook.md` says so.

## APRV-403 — a deferred drift record says so, and the retry names itself

Found while landing APRV-381: the daemon case that holds the append lockfile for a whole tick printed `append-refused  envelope.drift … (lock-timeout)`, which is true and reads as a lost record, while the next tick re-derived and appended it.

The drift scan takes APRV-381's split using APRV-381's own classifier — `core/audit.ts`'s `isTransientAppendError` over its closed list, imported rather than copied, so the two sweeps cannot come to disagree. Both append sites take it. The new `drift-deferred` warning names the task, carries the append error's own code, and says the record is not lost and the scan retries; the `drift` event gains `retry?: true` when this process deferred it, and `cli/daemon.ts` renders it.

**A defect found while landing this, fixed with it.** `writeBack` rewrote any file whose `state:` disagreed with the log, with no check that the drift record had actually been appended. Under contention it repaired the file while the record was deferred, so the next tick found the file agreeing with the log, the retry had nothing to re-derive, and the deferral resolved into silence — a correction made off the record, which is what SPEC §6.3's fixed order exists to prevent. Write-back now skips a file whose drift record this tick deferred.

Invariant 5 is untouched: nothing about the append changed. The record is still placed against the `expectedHead` of a read taken immediately before it, and a `head-moved` here *is* compare-and-append working. Deferring is the only answer that neither writes against a head the scan never saw nor loses the observation.

## APRV-425 — the live prompt on top, the dead ones in one message

`orderPending` is applied once per cycle: live requests newest first (live being younger than the hook's wait plus its retry grace, the same boundary the collapse uses), then stale ones oldest first, attestation prompts last where `buildPendingQueue` put them. `/queue` takes the same order. `supersededPending` collapses a pending request whose payload bytes and class a newer pending request also names — two askings of one question, of which only the newer has an asker — keyed by bytes and class because a harness adapter mints a fresh task id per tool call. `staleLines` now states whether each collapsed member is there for age or for supersession instead of claiming all of them are old.

A restart with N stale pending was a banner plus N prompts and is now **one summary and zero prompts**, with the next cycle of that process sending nothing. The sent-record is rebuilt from the log by the collapse itself and is never read as evidence: a collapsed request stays pending, is listed by `/queue`, and is decidable from any copy already on the phone through APRV-196's restart-stable action ref.

### One acceptance criterion is held, deliberately

**APRV-425 AC1's literal "zero new messages" is not claimed.** A listener cannot tell a request a previous process delivered from one that arrived while nothing was running — both predate its start — so withholding a re-delivery on age alone would produce the one outcome SPEC §10.3 forbids: a pending request nobody is shown. The one summary is what keeps it legal. The SPEC hunk literal zero would need is written out in APRV-425's implementation notes and **not applied**; it names evidence this project does not have (a delivery event in the log, or a read of the chat's own history), so it wants a human's call rather than a lane's.
